title: EDUCATION | 5.24.26 What I'm Refining After a Year of Explicit Instruction
author: Sol in the Wild
summary: After a full school year committing to explicit instruction, cognitive science, and a knowledge-building curriculum, the author reflects on what the Modal Model of Memory revealed about where learning was being lost -- and announces three areas of summer refinement. First, retrieval practice: the author found students could answer retrieval questions during Do Nows but couldn't use the same knowledge in reading, discussion, or writing -- a sign retrieval was occurring but automaticity had not been achieved. The refinement focuses on which knowledge deserves persistent retrieval, how often concepts are revisited, and how retrieval tasks mirror actual knowledge use. Second, curriculum sequence: lessons that went smoothest had strong prior knowledge foundations; lessons that struggled introduced too many unfamiliar elements simultaneously. Third, classroom routines and attention: small inefficiencies -- long directions, dragging transitions, weak response routines -- compete for working memory space and erode learning. The Modal Model of Memory, the author argues, is the clarifying lens that makes these otherwise diffuse problems diagnosable and actionable.
points: * The Modal Model of Memory -- tracking attention, working memory, encoding, retrieval, and long-term memory -- gave the author a diagnostic framework to identify where learning was being lost throughout the school year. * A critical gap was discovered between retrieval performance (students could answer Do Now questions) and knowledge automaticity (students struggled to use the same knowledge during complex reading, discussion, or writing tasks). * Summer retrieval refinement focuses on which knowledge must become automatic for future learning to work, how spacing and frequency of retrieval align to curriculum sequence, and whether retrieval tasks mirror how students will actually need to use knowledge. * Curriculum coherence matters more than previously understood: when knowledge builds effectively across lessons, students need less reteaching, less clarification, and less cognitive effort to acquire new information. * Classroom routine inefficiencies -- long directions, unstructured turn-and-talks, weak listening checks, excessive teacher talk -- directly compete for working memory space and must be designed for efficiency, attention, and automaticity.
quotes: The more this year went on, the more I realized how many instructional decisions need to connect back to memory and the cognitive architecture of how we learn.
Retrieval was happening, but the knowledge still wasn't automatic enough to support more complex thinking and transfer.
I want retrieval to feel less like isolated review for assessments and more like preparation for future thinking and learning.

I now know curriculum coherence matters far more than I understood a few years ago. When knowledge builds effectively, students need less reteaching, less clarification, and less cognitive effort to learn the new information.

Small inefficiencies cause big problems for learning: directions that are too long, transitions that drag, turn-and-talks without enough structure, weak response routines -- all of those things matter for learning because they compete for working memory space.
